q: RA 7279 sets an affordability cap for housing meant for average and low-income earners. Housing costs for such units should stay at or below what share of gross family income?
n: Affordability means housing costs no more than 30% of gross family income for average and low-income earners.

q: Under the ceiling in force since December 2025 (DHSUD-DEPDev JMC 2025-001), what is the maximum selling price of a socialized horizontal (subdivision) housing unit of 27 sq m or more?
ref: DHSUD-DEPDev JMC 2025-001 — Socialized Housing Price Ceiling
n: JMC 2025-001 raised the socialized housing ceiling to PHP 950,000 for horizontal units of 27 sq m and above, and PHP 844,440 for 24 to 26 sq m. The old PHP 400,000 ceiling is long superseded.

q: Under DHSUD-DEPDev JMC 2025-001, how high may the selling price of a socialized condominium (vertical) unit go?
ref: DHSUD-DEPDev JMC 2025-001 — Socialized Housing Price Ceiling
n: JMC 2025-001 sets socialized vertical housing between PHP 1.28 million and PHP 1.8 million, depending on the number of storeys and the unit size.

q: Which department sets housing price ceilings today, after HLURB was abolished in 2019?
ref: DHSUD-DEPDev JMC 2025-001 — Socialized Housing Price Ceiling
n: RA 11201 (2019) replaced HLURB with the Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development, which issues price ceilings jointly with DEPDev, the agency formerly called NEDA.

q: Housing that costs more than the socialized ceiling but is still meant for low-income buyers is classified as:
n: BP 220 covers two levels: socialized housing for the underprivileged and homeless, and economic housing for families of average income. Medium-cost and open-market housing sit above them.

q: Housing priced above the medium-cost range, sold with no price ceiling or subsidy, is classified as:
n: The ladder runs socialized, economic, low-cost, medium-cost, then open market, which carries no ceiling.

q: BP 220 lists the basic needs of human settlements. Which item below is NOT on that list?
ref: BP 220 — Basic Needs of Human Settlements
n: BP 220's revised rules list the basic needs of human settlements, in descending order, as water, movement and circulation, storm drainage, solid and liquid waste disposal, park/playground, and power. Telecommunications is not on that list.

q: What do you call housing projects the government carries out for underprivileged and homeless citizens?
n: Socialized housing is the government program for the underprivileged and homeless, with the lowest price ceiling.

q: Housing projects meant for families with average incomes are known as:
n: Economic housing serves average-income families, one step above socialized housing.

q: Under RA 7279, what term refers to the most reasonable price given the needs and capacity of the beneficiaries?
n: Affordable cost is the most reasonable price given what the beneficiaries need and can pay.

q: Which term describes a building designed or used as the home of one or more families?
n: A dwelling is any building designed or used as the home of one or more families.

q: What is a dwelling meant for only one family on each lot called?
n: A single-family dwelling holds one family on each lot.

q: One lot holds separate living units for several families, typically sharing access, services, and use of the land. What is this dwelling called?
n: A multiple-family dwelling holds separate units for several families on one lot, sharing access and services.

q: Facilities meant to serve shared needs and benefit the community as a whole are known as:
n: Community facilities serve the shared needs of the whole community, such as centers, schools and stores.

q: Multi-purpose centers, schools, and drugstores all fall under which category?
n: Multi-purpose centers, schools and drugstores are community facilities, allocated apart from parks and open space.

q: A one-family dwelling with open space on all sides is called a:
n: A single-detached dwelling stands alone with open space on all sides.

q: Two or more separate living units divided by party walls or firewalls make up which type of dwelling?
n: A duplex or single-attached dwelling has separate units divided by a firewall or party wall.

q: Which dwelling type is a single-attached building of three or more separate living units joined side by side and divided by party walls?
n: A rowhouse is three or more units side by side, divided by party walls, each with its own access.

q: A livable dwelling unit that already has all exterior walls, the floor, door and window openings, plumbing fixtures, and electrical wiring is called a:
n: A shell house has all exterior walls, the floor, door and window openings, plumbing fixtures and wiring.

q: What do you get when all windows, doors, and partition walls are added to a Shell House?
n: A complete house is a shell house plus all doors, windows and partition walls.

q: Under BP 220, what is the term for any wall that divides two adjoining living units?
n: BP 220 calls any wall dividing two adjoining living units a firewall.

q: A wall that two parties use together under an easement agreement is known as a:
n: A party wall is shared by two owners under an easement agreement.

q: BP 220 defines a party wall as a wall used jointly by two parties under an easement agreement. According to the same definition, where is such a wall erected?
o: Inside one owner's lot, set back from the line
Between two units on the same parcel
On the line between two separately owned parcels
Along the front line facing the street
n: BP 220 places the party wall on the line separating two parcels that are separate real estate.

q: Which term refers to a parcel of land bounded by streets on its sides and occupied by, or meant for, buildings?
n: A block is land bounded by streets and occupied by, or meant for, buildings.

q: A public way 2.00 meters wide that cuts through a block and connects to streets at both ends is called a(n):
n: An alley is a 2.00 m public way that breaks a long block and joins streets at both ends.

q: Among these BP 220 site elements, which one is NOT meant to give access to a property?
n: An alley only breaks up a long block; it is not a permitted means of access to a property.

q: In a socialized housing project, what is the public way used only for pedestrian access to a property?
n: A pathwalk is a 3.0 m public way for pedestrian access to lots, allowed only in socialized housing.

q: BP 220 sets the narrowest a pathwalk may be at:
n: Pathwalks must be at least 3.00 m wide.

q: What is the longest a pathwalk may run under BP 220?
n: Pathwalks may be no longer than 60 m.

q: In subdivision development, trees with a caliper diameter of at least ___ must be preserved.
n: Trees with a caliper of 200 mm or more must be preserved and worked into the site plan.

q: Which of these are among BP 220's planning considerations for subdivision design?
o: Observe easements set by other codes
Extend major streets for future links
n: All three are legitimate BP 220 subdivision-planning considerations, so there is no exception among them.

q: For socialized housing projects, what ratio of saleable to non-saleable lots does BP 220 require?
n: BP 220 sets no fixed saleable-to-non-saleable ratio; PD 957 caps saleable area at 70%.

q: Parks and playgrounds become required once a project's gross area reaches:
n: Parks and playgrounds are required once the project reaches 1 hectare.

q: How does BP 220 treat the area for parks and playgrounds versus the area for community facilities?
o: Parks and playgrounds count as part of the community facility area
Community facilities count as part of the parks and playground area
One may be provided in place of the other
n: Parks and playgrounds are allocated separately from, not included within, community facility areas.

q: Which of these may be counted toward a project's parks and playground allocation?
n: A basketball court is recreation and counts as park area; chapels, stalls and parking do not.

q: What is the absolute smallest area permitted for parks and playgrounds?
ref: Revised IRR of BP 220 — Parks and playgrounds table
n: No park and playground area may be smaller than 100 sqm.

q: At what density (lots or living units per hectare) must 3.5% of a project's gross area go to parks and playgrounds?
ref: Revised IRR of BP 220 — Parks and playgrounds table
n: Densities of 150 lots or units per hectare and below set aside 3.5% of the gross area.

q: A project with a density of how many lots or living units per hectare must set aside 4% of its gross area for parks and playgrounds?
ref: Revised IRR of BP 220 — Parks and playgrounds table
n: Densities of 151 to 160 per hectare set aside 4%.

q: Parks and playgrounds take up 5% of gross area when project density falls within which range (lots or living units per hectare)?
ref: Revised IRR of BP 220 — Parks and playgrounds table
n: Densities of 161 to 175 per hectare set aside 5%.

q: Match the allocation: 6% of gross area for parks and playgrounds applies at a density (lots or living units per hectare) of:
ref: Revised IRR of BP 220 — Parks and playgrounds table
n: Densities of 176 to 200 per hectare set aside 6%.

q: Which density range (lots or living units per hectare) calls for 7% of a project's gross area as parks and playgrounds?
ref: Revised IRR of BP 220 — Parks and playgrounds table
n: Densities of 201 to 225 per hectare set aside 7%.

q: At what density (lots or living units per hectare) does the parks and playground allocation start at 9% of gross area, plus 1% for every additional 10 lots or living units or fraction thereof?
ref: Revised IRR of BP 220 — Parks and playgrounds table
n: Above 225 per hectare the share is 9%, plus 1% for every further 10 lots or fraction.

q: Besides parks and playgrounds, which facility must also be provided in projects of 1 hectare or more, whether socialized or economic?
n: A neighborhood multi-purpose center is mandatory for projects of 1 hectare or more, socialized or economic.
